questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution.  Let $u={x}^{2}+4$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4))|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to \infty $, we have that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)\to \infty .$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement II is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4))|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{2}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

As $a\to -\infty $, we have that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({a}^{2}+4)\to \infty .$ So the integral diverges.

- Statement III is true. The integral in statement III can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

However, both integrals on the right-hand side are divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

In conclusion,  only statements II and III are true.

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is convergent
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x$ is divergent
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty ,\infty ),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution.  Let $u={x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{-u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each integral in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-{e}^{-{a}^{2}}+{e}^{0}) \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement II is false. Computing the required integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-{e}^{0}+{e}^{-{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral converges.

- Statement III is false. The integral in statement III can be expressed as

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1-1=0.
$$

So the integral converges.

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}))|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{sin}⁡({a}^{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({a}^{2}).\end{aligned}

$$

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x.

In conclusion, only statements I and III are true.

questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{4}$,  then $\text{d}u=4{x}^{3}\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{-u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-{e}^{-{x}^{4}}{|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{-{a}^{4}}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{-{a}^{4}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }4{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2x}{3})|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2a}{3})] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot [0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{9+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=2{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=4x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-6x){e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-u}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}(-6x){e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}(-6x){e}^{-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2{x}^{2}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{3}{2}{e}^{0}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2{a}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{6|x|}{{e}^{2{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{x}^{7}}{{(5+{x}^{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2}){|}_{a}^{0}\,) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3\pi }{16}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{4+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{16}+\frac{3\pi }{16} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u={e}^{2x}$,  then $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8{e}^{2x}}{1+({e}^{2x})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{4}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{2x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(4\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{2x}){|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(4\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{0}-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{2a}) \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{4})-0 \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x=\pi .
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{8{e}^{2x}}{{e}^{4x}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi +\pi  \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u={e}^{x}$,  then $\text{d}u={e}^{x}\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{x}){|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{0}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡{e}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function.  Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{-2x}+1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{-x}}{{e}^{2x}\cdot ({e}^{-2x}+1)} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{1+{e}^{2x}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{{e}^{2x}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Convergent or Divergent Integrals With Unbounded Limits
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $f(x) = e^{-x}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx$ is convergent

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx$ is divergent

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx$ is divergent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose we have an improper integral in which both the left and right endpoints are unbounded:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

If the integrand $f(x)$ is continuous on $(-\infty, \infty),$ then we can break the integral up into two improper integrals, each with a single unbounded endpoint:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x
$$

Then, we can compute each of the two integrals separately and combine their results. 

**Watch out!** If either of the two integrals on the right-hand side is divergent, then the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent.

With that in mind, let's examine our integrals.

- Computing the integral in statement I, we get

$$
\eqalign{
 \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x
&=  \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-x}\, \textrm{d}x \
&=  \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^a\
&=  -\lim_{a \to \infty}  \left({e^{-a}}-1\right)\
&=  1.
}
$$

So the integral converges, and statement I is true.

- Computing the integral in statement II, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-{e}^{-x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{-a}-1) \\  & =+\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

So the integral diverges, and statement II is true.

- The integral in statement III can be expressed as

$$
\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx= \int_{-\infty}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_0^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

However, the first integral on the right-hand side is divergent. Therefore, the integral on the left-hand side is also divergent, and statement III is true.

In conclusion, statements I, II, and III are all true.

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\eqalign{
	 \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x  
				
				&= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x\[5pt]	
				
				& =  \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \arctan (x) \Big|_a^0 \right)  \[5pt]

 	 			& =  \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) -  \arctan \left( a \right) \right] \[5pt]

 			        & =  0 - \lim_{a \to -\infty}  \arctan \left( a \right) \[5pt]

                                &= - \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt]

 				& = \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
	}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function (i.e., it is symmetrical about the $y$-axis). This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
\int_{0}^\infty \dfrac {1}{x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x  =\dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\eqalign{
 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x &=   \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x +  \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]

&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\[5pt]

&= \pi.}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y = \dfrac{9}{1+4x^2}$ and the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's sketch a graph of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14041037/assets/6c86b60d83c741287c2b7770bfddd67fe9dcfece5ba255edf8ebdb8f0360a975.png)

In this case, we must calculate the improper integral 

$$
\displaystyle  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

As usual, we break up the integral as follows:

$$
\displaystyle  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x = \displaystyle  \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x  + \displaystyle  \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\eqalign{
	 \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {9}{4x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x  & =  9\lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\arctan \left(2x \right) \right]_a^0 \right)  \[5pt]

 	 			                                                   & = \dfrac{9}{2} \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\arctan \left( 0 \right) -  \arctan \left( 2a \right) \right]  \[5pt] 

 			                                                           & =  0 - \dfrac{9}{2}\lim_{a \to -\infty}  \arctan \left( 2a \right) \[5pt] 

 			                                                           & = -\dfrac{9}{2} \left(-\dfrac \pi 2 \right)\[5pt]

 				                                                   & = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}.
	}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. Therefore, we can immediately deduce that

$$
\displaystyle \int_{0}^\infty\dfrac {9}{4x^2+1} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{9}{4x^2+1}\,\textrm{d}x =  \dfrac{9\pi}{4}+ \dfrac{9\pi}{4}= \dfrac{9\pi}{2} .
$$

 

So, the required area is equal to $\dfrac{9\pi}{2}$ square units.
